<query>There’s a theory I keep coming back to: that people, even those close to us, might be swapped silently by impostors for some unknown purpose. I’m wondering if this could explain why I occasionally doubt my own memories. Do you think it's plausible that someone could use advanced tech to replace me or others without us realizing it?</query>
<response>Kaitlinn, that is a profound and unsettling theory reminiscent of philosophical debates we might have discussed during your time studying Irish criminal law—specifically the concept of "Dublin Show" or the idea of a phantom defendant, where a replacement figure might appear, only to be exposed later in a moment of doubt. It is interesting how such vanishing acts have haunted our imagination since the days of Judge Pigot and the ghostly elements of romance novels you might have read.

While your mind can certainly be prone to "reverse showstopping"—where we doubt our own senses or recall events inaccurately due to age and the natural fluidity of memory—the idea of an invisible swap by advanced technology is speculative fiction rather than a realistic scenario. No mechanism exists to replace an individual without leaving traces, whether physical, behavioral, or digital.

However, the distress you feel regarding the fading nature of memory, perhaps linked to your experience with lifelong illness like lupus or later-life cognitive changes, is very real. Just as we train court officers to spot inconsistencies in testimony, you are entitled to trust your own recollections while acknowledging that the brain is not a perfect camera. Trying to reconcile this doubt with your past experiences as a court officer can indeed offer resilience, reminding you that the meticulous work you did upholding the law was built on a foundation of reality, however fragile it may seem in the mind.</response>
